shots.title: SINCE 1962
shots.body: NAVY F4H + AIR FORCE F-110 → ONE NAME

caps.text: F.
Fighter.
It's the most famous letter in military aviation, and today it covers multirole jets that also strike targets on the ground.
The F-35 should have been the F-24, the next number in line.
Instead, it kept the number of its demonstrator, the X-35.
And the F-117 Nighthawk got an F, even though it was built for ground attack.
A.
Attack.
An attack aircraft is built to hit targets on land or at sea.
Today, the A-10 is the only aircraft in the Air Force that still carries a plain A.
B.
Bomber.
Bombers fly long-range strike missions.
The newest one is the B-21.
Its number was chosen because it's the first bomber of the twenty-first century.
By the rules, it would have been the B-3.
C.
Cargo.
C means transport, like the C-130 Hercules.
And the C-130 shows how the whole system works.
Add one more letter in front, and the same airframe becomes a gunship, a rescue plane, a special operations plane, an electronic warfare plane, or a tanker.
K.
Tanker.
Put a K in front of a C, and you get a tanker, like the KC-46.
K exists as a basic mission too, but no ordinary aircraft has ever been given it the way the rules intended.
Some names simply copy the maker.
A tanker sold to other countries became the KC-767, straight from Boeing's model number.
E.
Electronic.
As a modified mission, E means electronic warfare, like the EC-130.
As a basic mission, it means special electronics, for aircraft built around radars and sensors.
H.
Rescue, and helicopter.
H can show up twice in the same name.
In the HH-60G, the first H means search and rescue, and the second H means helicopter.
Many of them started life as Black Hawks that were modified for rescue.
M.
Multi-mission.
M aircraft fly combat and special operations, like the MC-130.
And the MQ-9 Reaper reads as multi-mission, unmanned, design number nine.
U.
Utility.
U aircraft fly support missions, like the UH-60 Black Hawk.
Utility was once used as a cover.
The U-2 spy plane was labeled utility to hide what it really did.
R.
Reconnaissance.
R is for spy missions.
The SR-71 Blackbird was set to be called the RS-71, but Air Force chief Curtis LeMay preferred SR, for strategic reconnaissance.
And SR is what stuck.
W.
Weather.
W means weather reconnaissance.
That's why the Air Force's hurricane hunters are WC-130s.
V.
VIP, and vertical takeoff.
In front, V means VIP transport.
The President's 747 is the VC-25, and his newest helicopter is the VH-92.
Before the dash, V means vertical or short takeoff, like the MV-22 Osprey.
L.
Cold weather.
L means modified for cold weather.
The LC-130 has skis, for landing on ice.
Q.
Unmanned.
Q means drone.
There's even a letter for the ground stations that fly them: D, for the U A V control segment.
P.
Patrol.
P means maritime patrol, for aircraft that watch the sea.
Today's main one is the P-8 Poseidon, a Navy jet built on a Boeing 737.
S.
Anti-submarine.
S is for hunting submarines.
Before the dash, S means something completely different: a spaceplane.
The S-3 Viking flew from aircraft carriers to hunt submarines.
T.
Trainer.
The T-6 Texan Two skipped the numbers four and five, as a tribute to the original T-6 trainer.
O.
Observation.
O means observation, like spotting targets for other aircraft.
The new OA-1K Skyraider Two borrowed the name of the old A-1 Skyraider.
X.
Experimental.
In front of everything, X means experimental.
That's where the F-35 started, as the X-35.
Experimental aircraft flown by manufacturers or by NASA often get X numbers too.
Y.
Prototype.
The jet that won the competition was the YF-22.
The one that entered service was the F-22.
G.
Grounded.
As a prefix, G means permanently grounded.
Before the dash, G means glider.
J and N.
Special test.
J means a temporary special test, and the aircraft goes back to normal service.
N means it never does.
The whole system dates to nineteen sixty-two.
Before that, the Navy and the Air Force named their aircraft differently, and the same fighter was the F4H Phantom to one and the F-110 to the other.
After the change, it became simply the F-4.
And after the letters come the numbers.
In nineteen sixty-two, the counts were restarted, which is why they suddenly got small again.
The last letter marks the version: A, then B, then C.
I and O are skipped, so they're never confused with one and zero.
And the number thirteen has been skipped in many series, for superstition.
Which aircraft name should I decode next?
Tell me in the comments.
